mcqs.question: An AS receives a BGP route advertisement whose AS-path already contains its own AS number. What should it do, and why?
options: Accept the route anyway, since AS-path is only used for reporting purposes
Automatically promote that route to highest local preference
Forward the route unchanged to all its own neighbors
Discard the route, since seeing its own AS number in the path means accepting it would create a routing loop
mcqs.explanation: The AS-path doubles as BGP's built-in loop prevention: if an AS's own number already appears in the path, accepting it would mean routing back through itself, so it's discarded. AS-path isn't merely informational (the reporting-only claim is false), forwarding a self-referential loop onward would propagate the problem (the forward-unchanged approach), and there's no rule auto-boosting such a route's preference (the auto-promote-preference claim is false).

mcqs.question: Two BGP routes exist to the same destination: one with a shorter AS-path but lower local preference, another with a longer AS-path but higher local preference (set by policy). Which does BGP prefer?
options: The higher local-preference route, since local preference is evaluated before AS-path length in BGP's decision process
The shorter AS-path route, since path length is always BGP's first tie-breaker
Whichever route was received most recently
BGP cannot choose between them and will drop both routes
mcqs.explanation: Local preference is checked before AS-path length in BGP's best-path selection process, meaning a deliberate policy decision overrides raw path length — reflecting that BGP optimizes for business/policy considerations first. Path length is not the first criterion (the path-length-first claim is false), recency of receipt isn't a tie-breaker in this process (the most-recently-received tie-breaker), and BGP does select a single best path rather than dropping both (the drop-both claim is false).

mcqs.question: Why can an AS accidentally cause a major, wide-reaching internet outage just by misconfiguring a BGP announcement?
options: BGP requires cryptographic proof of address ownership before any route is accepted, so misconfigurations are automatically blocked
BGP has no built-in verification that an AS advertising a prefix actually owns that address space, so other networks can end up believing and routing traffic based on the false announcement
BGP misconfigurations only ever affect the misconfiguring AS's own internal network, never the wider internet
Major outages from BGP misconfiguration are only theoretical and have never actually occurred
mcqs.explanation: The root vulnerability is the lack of built-in origin verification — by default, BGP trusts announcements at face value, so a bad or malicious announcement can be believed and propagated widely. RPKI exists specifically because that verification is missing (the cryptographic-proof-by-default claim is false), the effects are not contained to the originating AS (the effects-contained-locally claim is false), and such incidents have genuinely occurred and caused real, large-scale outages (the theoretical-only claim is false).
